title: Fields and finite fields
objectives: Prove that the integers modulo a prime form a field.

screens.title: Where is the 1
screens.prose: Left: the non-zero part of the multiplication table of $\mathbb{Z}_7$. Right: the same for $\mathbb{Z}_6$. A 1 in row $a$ marks an inverse of $a$.
screens.question: Tap the 1 in each row of $\mathbb{Z}_7$, on the left.

hints.text: Every row of the left table has exactly one 1.

feedback.correct: Right. Every non-zero element of $\mathbb{Z}_7$ has an inverse.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap one cell per row of the left table: the one that reads 1.

explain.text: Each row of $\mathbb{Z}_7$ holds one 1, so each non-zero element has an inverse. On the right, rows 2, 3 and 4 of $\mathbb{Z}_6$ hold no 1. There $2 \times 3 = 0$.

screens.title: The inverses mod 7
screens.prose: Read the inverses from the left table. In $\mathbb{Z}_6$ on the right, look at row 2: it reads 2, 4, 0, 2, 4.
screens.question: Give the inverse of each element of $\mathbb{Z}_7$.

hints.text: Find the column where row $a$ reads 1.

feedback.correct: Right. $2 \leftrightarrow 4$, $3 \leftrightarrow 5$ and 6 is its own inverse.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each answer times $a$ must leave remainder 1 mod 7.

explain.text: $2 \times 4 = 8$, $3 \times 5 = 15$ and $6 \times 6 = 36$ all leave remainder 1 mod 7. In $\mathbb{Z}_6$, row 2 never reaches 1. And $2 \times 3 = 6 \equiv 0$.

screens.title: Integral domains and fields
screens.prose: An **integral domain** is a commutative ring with $1 \ne 0$ and no zero divisors. A **field** is a commutative ring with $1 \ne 0$ in which every non-zero element is a unit. A unit is never a zero divisor (l14), so every field is an integral domain.
screens.question: What is $\mathbb{Z}_6$?

options.text: A commutative ring that is not an integral domain, since $2 \times 3 = 0$.
A field, since it is a ring with six elements.
options.why: You counted elements. Row 2 has no 1, so 2 has no inverse.

options.text: An integral domain that is not a field.
options.why: An integral domain has no zero divisors, and $2 \times 3 = 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_6$.
$\mathbb{Z}_6$ is a ring (l14); it simply has zero divisors.

hints.text: Look for a product of non-zero elements equal to 0.

feedback.correct: Right. $\mathbb{Z}_7$ is a field; $\mathbb{Z}_6$ is not even an integral domain.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check for zero divisors first.

explain.text: $2 \times 3 = 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_6$, so it has zero divisors. It is a commutative ring but not an integral domain, and so not a field. $\mathbb{Z}_7$ has an inverse for every non-zero element: it is a field.

screens.title: Residues mod a prime form a field
screens.prose: From l3: $a$ has an inverse mod $n$ exactly when $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, by Euclid's algorithm. Use it to prove $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is a field for a prime $p$.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is a commutative ring with $1 \ne 0$, as $p \ge 2$ (l14).
The only positive divisors of $p$ are 1 and $p$, and $p \nmid a$; so $\gcd(a, p) = 1$ (definition of prime).
So $a$ has an inverse mod $p$ (l3: Euclid's algorithm).
Every non-zero element is a unit, so $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is a field (definition).

lines.why: Being smaller is not enough: $\gcd(4, 6) = 2$ though $4 < 6$. The primality of $p$ is what makes the gcd 1.

hints.text: Take a non-zero $a$ and find its gcd with $p$.
A prime's only divisors are 1 and $p$.
$\gcd(a, p) = 1$ gives an inverse by l3.

feedback.correct: Right. Primality gives $\gcd(a, p) = 1$, and l3 gives the inverse.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Show $\gcd(a, p) = 1$, then use l3.

byKey.d1: You used $a < p$ alone. $\gcd(4, 6) = 2$ shows that is not enough; primality is needed.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: For $0 < a < p$, the gcd of $a$ and $p$ divides $p$ and is not $p$. So it is 1, and $a$ has an inverse. Every non-zero element is a unit: $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is a field.

screens.title: Finite integral domains are fields
screens.prose: No gcd is needed when the ring is finite. Let $D$ be a finite integral domain and fix $a \ne 0$. Prove $a$ has an inverse. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Define $m : D \to D$ by $m(x) = ax$ (multiply by $a$).
$a \ne 0$ and $D$ has no zero divisors, so $x - y = 0$: $m$ is injective.
An injective map of a finite set to itself is onto (counting).
So some $x$ has $ax = 1$, and $a$ is a unit (onto).
$m$ is onto because it is a homomorphism.
lines.why: Onto does not come from structure; $x \mapsto 2x$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ is not onto. It comes from finiteness.

hints.text: No zero divisors makes the map injective.
Finite plus injective gives onto, so 1 is hit.

feedback.correct: Right. Finiteness turns injective into onto.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Show $x \mapsto ax$ is injective, then use that $D$ is finite.

byKey.d1: You took onto from structure. On $\mathbb{Z}$, $x \mapsto 2x$ keeps addition and misses 1; finiteness is what gives onto.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: Multiplying by $a \ne 0$ is injective, because $a(x - y) = 0$ forces $x = y$. On a finite set, injective means onto. So $ax = 1$ for some $x$.

screens.title: Composite moduli fail
screens.prose: Now let $n = ab$ with $1 < a, b < n$, as for $6 = 2 \times 3$. Show that $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is not a field.
screens.question: Put the proof in order.

lines.text: $a \ne 0$ and $b \ne 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_n$, since $1 < a, b < n$.
A unit is never a zero divisor (l14), so $a$ is not a unit.

hints.text: A zero divisor cannot be a unit.

feedback.correct: Right. $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is a field exactly when $n$ is prime.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a zero divisor, then use l14.

explain.text: $a$ and $b$ are non-zero but $ab \equiv 0$, so $a$ is a zero divisor. A unit is never a zero divisor. So $a$ has no inverse and $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is not a field.

screens.title: Which are fields
screens.prose: Combine the last two proofs: $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is a field exactly when $n$ is prime.
screens.question: For which $n$ from 1 to 12 is $\mathbb{Z}_n$ a field? Select all that apply.

options.why: You kept 4. $2 \times 2 = 4 \equiv 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_4$, so 2 has no inverse.
$\mathbb{Z}_1$ is the zero ring, where $1 = 0$; a field needs $1 \ne 0$.

hints.text: A factorisation in the table rules $n$ out.
The blank columns are the primes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep exactly the $n$ with no factorisation into smaller factors.

explain.text: Each composite $n$ has a factorisation giving a zero divisor. Each prime gives a field. So the fields are $\mathbb{Z}_2$, $\mathbb{Z}_3$, $\mathbb{Z}_5$, $\mathbb{Z}_7$ and $\mathbb{Z}_{11}$.

screens.title: Solving in a field
screens.prose: In a field we can divide. Solve $3x + 4 \equiv 2 \pmod 7$: subtract 4, then multiply by $3^{-1} = 5$ from the table.
screens.question: What is $x$ in $\mathbb{Z}_7$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Reduce $3x \equiv 5$, then multiply by 5.

byKey.raw: You stopped at 25. Reduce it mod 7.
byKey.div: You stopped at $3x \equiv 5$ and read off 5. Multiply by $3^{-1} = 5$ to free $x$.

explain.text: $3x \equiv 5$, and multiplying by $3^{-1} = 5$ gives $x \equiv 25 \equiv 4$. Check: $3 \times 4 + 4 = 16 \equiv 2 \pmod 7$. Every linear equation $ax = b$ with $a \ne 0$ has one solution in a field.

screens.title: The field with four elements
screens.prose: Is $\mathbb{Z}_4$ the field with four elements? Left: $\mathbb{Z}_4$, where $2 \times 2 = 0$. Right: $\mathbb{F}_4 = \{0, 1, \alpha, \alpha + 1\}$, with $\alpha^2 = \alpha + 1$ and $1 + 1 = 0$. Finite fields have prime power sizes (Pinter chapter 27).
screens.question: Which is a field?

options.text: Only $\mathbb{F}_4$: each non-zero row has a 1, as $\alpha(\alpha + 1) = 1$.

options.why: You took $\mathbb{Z}_4$ for the field. $2 \times 2 = 0$ there, so 2 is a zero divisor.

options.text: Both: they have the same size.
options.why: Size is not enough. $\mathbb{Z}_4$ has a zero divisor; $\mathbb{F}_4$ has none.

options.text: Neither: there is no field with four elements.
options.why: $4 = 2^2$ is a prime power, and $\mathbb{F}_4$ on the right is one.

hints.text: Look for a 1 in every non-zero row.

feedback.correct: Right. The field with four elements is $\mathbb{F}_4$, not $\mathbb{Z}_4$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check row 2 of the left table for a 1.

byKey.z4: You took $\mathbb{Z}_4$. It has $2 \times 2 = 0$, so it is not even an integral domain.

explain.text: $\mathbb{Z}_4$ has $2 \times 2 = 0$, so it is not a field. In $\mathbb{F}_4$, $\alpha(\alpha + 1) = 1$ and $(\alpha + 1)^2 = \alpha$, and every non-zero row holds a 1. A field of size $n$ exists exactly when $n$ is a prime power.

screens.title: Splitting a signing key
screens.prose: A firm splits a signing key among 3 desk heads. Any 2 can recover it; one alone cannot. Over $\mathbb{Z}_{11}$ it picks the line $f(x) = 7 + 3x$; the secret is $f(0) = 7$. The shares are $(1, 10)$, $(2, 2)$ and $(3, 5)$. Two shares fix the line, since we can divide in a field.
screens.question: Recover the line from two pairs of shares.

hints.text: From B and C the slope is $(5 - 2)/(3 - 2) = 3$.
From A and C the slope is $(5 - 10)/(3 - 1) = -5 \times 2^{-1}$, with $2^{-1} = 6$.

feedback.correct: Right. Both pairs give the line $7 + 3x$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slope is the change in $f$ over the change in $x$; divide by multiplying by an inverse mod 11.

byKey.slope: You gave the slope. The secret is the value at $x = 0$.

explain.text: B and C give slope 3 and secret $2 - 6 \equiv 7$. A and C give slope $-5 \times 6 = -30 \equiv 3$, the same line. Over $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$ this breaks, since 2 has no inverse there.

ideas: A field is a commutative ring with $1 \ne 0$ where every non-zero element is a unit. An integral domain only asks for no zero divisors.
$\mathbb{Z}_n$ is a field exactly when $n$ is prime. Every finite integral domain is a field, because $x \mapsto ax$ is injective and so onto.
Finite fields have prime power sizes. The field with 4 elements is $\mathbb{F}_4 = \{0, 1, \alpha, \alpha + 1\}$, not $\mathbb{Z}_4$.

formula.name: Field test for residues
formula.tex: \mathbb{Z}_n \text{ is a field} \iff n \text{ is prime}
formula.note: Composite $n = ab$ gives the zero divisor $a$.

summary.trap: Taking $\mathbb{Z}_4$ for the field with four elements: $2 \times 2 = 0$ there.

quiz.prose: In the proof that $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is a field we used $\gcd(a, p) = 1$ for $0 < a < p$.
quiz.question: Why is the gcd 1?

options.text: The only positive divisors of $p$ are 1 and $p$, and $p$ does not divide $a$.

options.why: $p = 2$ is prime and even, and $\gcd(3, 9) = 3$ with 9 odd.
It returns the gcd, which is 2 for 4 and 6.

feedback.correct: Right. Primality leaves no other common divisor.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the divisors of $p$.

explain.text: Any common divisor of $a$ and $p$ divides $p$, so it is 1 or $p$. It is not $p$, as $0 < a < p$. So $\gcd(a, p) = 1$.

quiz.prose: Over $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$, the shares $(1, 0)$ and $(3, 6)$ fit both $7 + 3x$ and $2 + 8x$.
quiz.question: Why does two-share recovery fail here?

options.text: $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$ is not a field: the slope needs $2^{-1}$, and 2 has no inverse mod 10.
Two shares are never enough to fix a line.
options.why: Over $\mathbb{Z}_{11}$ two shares fixed the line. The trouble is the ring, not the count.
Both candidate secrets, 7 and 2, are residues mod 10.

options.text: 10 is even, and shares need an odd modulus.
options.why: Parity is not the point. Over $\mathbb{Z}_9$, shares at $x = 1$ and $x = 4$ fail too, since 3 has no inverse.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the slope $(6 - 0)/(3 - 1)$ mod 10.

explain.text: The slope solves $2m \equiv 6 \pmod{10}$, which has two solutions, 3 and 8. So the secret could be 7 or 2. Over a field, $2m = 6$ has exactly one solution.

quiz.prose: $\mathbb{Z}_2 = \{0, 1\}$ is the smallest field. In a field of characteristic $p$, adding 1 to itself $p$ times gives 0.
quiz.question: In $\mathbb{F}_4$, what is $\alpha + \alpha$?

options.why: $\mathbb{F}_4$ has only $0, 1, \alpha, \alpha + 1$. Its characteristic is 2, so $1 + 1 = 0$.
You squared instead of adding. $\alpha + \alpha$ is a sum.

feedback.correct: Right. Characteristic 2: every element is its own negative.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Factor out $\alpha$ and use $1 + 1 = 0$.

explain.text: $\alpha + \alpha = (1 + 1)\alpha$ by distributivity. In $\mathbb{F}_4$, $1 + 1 = 0$, so the sum is 0. Every element of a field of characteristic 2 is its own negative.
